pullRequest.title: feat: support parsing logical decoding messages from XLogData payload
pullRequest.body:
This is the start of a series of stacked PRs to support replaying DDL on destination shards (#1603). I'm breaking this up as it's overall a relatively big, somewhat complex change, and I'm curious how the split will affect reviewability. 

This PR adds support for parsing [logical decoding messages](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/protocol-logicalrep-message-formats.html#PROTOCOL-LOGICALREP-MESSAGE-FORMATS-MESSAGE) (stemming from [`pg_logical_emit_message`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-admin.html)), so that we can inject custom messages in the WAL, which allows us to perform custom functionality at specific LSNs in the WAL (at the exact point at which a DDL statement occurs), as well as receive custom data we don't otherwise have from native Postgres, which we can provide with custom event triggers containing `pg_logical_emit_message` calls.

No behavior is changed here.

Usage will be in a follow up PR, specifically for custom messages that will include the **actual** SQL for DDL occurrences that we wish to replay. Currently, we only have [`Relation`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/protocol-logicalrep-message-formats.html#PROTOCOL-LOGICALREP-MESSAGE-FORMATS-RELATION) to rely on for information about DDL. While that tells us the table's new columns, it doesn't give us what we need to figure out the exact SQL that was run.

pullRequest.title: fix: don't grant pg_monitor SELECT on queue/archive tables (#594)
pullRequest.body:
## Problem

Fixes #594. Since the `pg_monitor` grants were added, installing pgmq runs:

```sql
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA pgmq TO pg_monitor;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA pgmq TO pg_monitor;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA pgmq GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO pg_monitor;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA pgmq GRANT SELECT ON SEQUENCES TO pg_monitor;
```

That gives every `pg_monitor` member read access to **all** queue and archive tables,
i.e. full message payloads and headers. `pg_monitor` is meant for monitoring views and
functions, not application data, so this is an unintended data exposure. Monitoring only
needs whole-queue aggregates (`pgmq.metrics` / `pgmq.metrics_all`) and the queue list.

## Fix: column-level grants (no SECURITY DEFINER)

As suggested by @ChuckHend on the issue, `pg_monitor` is granted only the minimum the
monitoring functions read:

- `USAGE` on schema `pgmq` and `SELECT` on `pgmq.meta` (for `list_queues` / `metrics_all`) — unchanged.
- **Column-level** `SELECT (vt, enqueued_at)` on each queue table — the only columns
  `metrics()` / `metrics_all()` read (`count(*)`, `count(... vt <= now())`,
  `min/max(enqueued_at)`). `count(*)` is satisfied by column-level SELECT.
- `SELECT` on each queue's `_msg_id_seq` (for `total_messages`).

`message` / `headers` and the archive (`a_*`) tables are never granted to `pg_monitor`.
`metrics()` is unchanged from upstream (`SECURITY INVOKER`); there is **no SECURITY DEFINER
code** in pgmq. Grants are applied in `create_non_partitioned`, `create_unlogged` and
`create_partitioned` via `EXECUTE FORMAT('... ON pgmq.%I ...')` (identifier-safe). For
partitioned queues the grant on the parent is sufficient — metrics query the parent and the
privilege check happens there.

> Note: an earlier draft of this PR used a `SECURITY DEFINER` metrics function; it was
> dropped because a queue-creating role could plant a view/type/RLS policy that the definer
> would execute with the owner's privileges (privilege escalation). Column grants avoid that
> class of problem entirely.

## Upgrade path

`sql/pgmq--1.13.0--1.13.1.sql` (the unreleased version) now, in addition to the notify fix:

1. Removes the schema default privileges that granted `SELECT` to `pg_monitor` (for every
   grantor role).
2. Revokes the old broad `SELECT` from `pg_monitor` on every relation in `pgmq` except
   `meta` — queue/archive tables, partitioned parents and pg_partman children, sequences,
   and any user-added views/matviews/foreign tables over them.
3. `CREATE OR REPLACE`s the three queue-creation functions so queues created after the
   upgrade also get the column grants.
4. Backfills the column-level `SELECT (vt, enqueued_at)` + sequence `SELECT` for every
   existing queue in `pgmq.meta`.
5. Warns (never fails) if a whole-table `SELECT` for `pg_monitor` remains — e.g. a grant
   made `WITH GRANT OPTION` by a role the upgrade cannot act as, which `REVOKE` silently
   skips.

The migration is idempotent and fail-open: if the upgrading role cannot revoke/grant on an
object (not its owner), it emits a `WARNING` with the exact statement to run manually rather
than aborting `ALTER EXTENSION UPDATE`.

## pg_dump parity

The maintainer noted fresh-install vs. upgraded users could end up with different `pg_dump`
output. Because both paths now apply the **same** explicit per-queue column/sequence grants
(and neither creates schema default ACLs), a fresh install and an upgraded install produce
identical `pgmq` ACLs. Verified: `pg_dump -n pgmq --schema-only` of a fresh 1.13.1 install
and a 1.13.0→1.13.1 upgrade (same queues) are byte-identical except for pg18's random
`\restrict`/`\unrestrict` dump tokens.

Residual note: parity holds when the grantor role is the same. If pre-existing queues were
owned by different roles, the recorded grantor in each ACL entry can differ between installs;
this is inherent to per-object grants and does not change the effective privileges.

## Behavior change for operators

This is an intentional, security-relevant behavior change: after installing/upgrading,
`pg_monitor` members can no longer `SELECT` from queue or archive tables (or their
`message` / `headers` columns). Anything that relied on `pg_monitor` to read queue rows
directly will now get `permission denied` and should use `pgmq.metrics()` /
`pgmq.metrics_all()` / `pgmq.list_queues()` instead, or be granted access explicitly.

## Metrics still work

Verified on PostgreSQL 18.4 and 14.23: a `pg_monitor` member can run `pgmq.metrics()`,
`pgmq.metrics_all()` and `pgmq.list_queues()`, and can read `vt` / `enqueued_at` and the
sequence, while `SELECT * / message FROM pgmq.q_*`, `SELECT * FROM pgmq.a_*`, and
`pgmq.read(...)` are all denied with `permission denied`.

## Tests

`test/sql/base.sql` (+ `expected/base.out`) now assert, for a `pg_monitor` member:
`metrics` / `metrics_all` / `list_queues` succeed and `vt,enqueued_at` + the sequence are
readable, while the whole queue table, the `message` column, the archive table and `read()`
are denied; a role that is neither `pg_monitor` nor able to read the queue table is denied
`metrics`; the fresh install creates no `pg_default_acl` for the schema; and there is no
`SECURITY DEFINER` function in schema `pgmq`.

`make installcheck` (regression: base, fifo_per_group, fifo_rr, fifo, topic; isolation:
transaction_tests) passes on PostgreSQL 18.4. The upgrade was additionally validated by a
real `ALTER EXTENSION pgmq UPDATE '1.13.0' -> '1.13.1'` (old broad access before, denied
after; new post-upgrade queues get the column grants) and by re-running the migration for
idempotency.

pullRequest.title: perf(cargo): skip crates whose store slot is already complete
pullRequest.body:
## Summary

A repeat `pnpm install` in a Cargo workspace ran the full materialize pipeline for every crate in `Cargo.lock`: a store-index lookup and integrity check per crate, a regenerated `.cargo-checksum.json`, and a forced re-import of the slot. On this repository that was about 2.6 s of a 3.6 s no-op install (pnpm/tasks#69).

The install now probes each crate's store slot for its completion marker before touching the registry or the store index. `import_indexed_dir` places `.cargo-checksum.json` last, so a slot whose manifest names the lockfile's checksum is a finished import and is linked as it is. Only the remaining crates go through download and import, and the registry configuration is fetched only when at least one crate needs it, so an offline repeat install with a warm store asks the registry for nothing. `pnpm install --force` re-materializes every crate, the way it re-materializes npm packages. Closes pnpm/tasks#69.

The checksum manifest is now an explicit completion marker in the importer. It used to be the marker only by sorting first among a crate's files, which fails for crates that ship a file such as `.appveyor.yml`; an interrupted import of such a crate could have left a slot that looked finished. The git vendoring path, which already probed the manifest, now shares the probe.

### Measurements

Warm `pnpm install --offline` with every crate already in the store, on a Cargo workspace with 771 registry crates in `Cargo.lock` (this repository's `[workspace.dependencies]` as one package's dependencies; 2.4 GB of unpacked crates in the store). macOS, APFS, `hyperfine`, 5 to 10 runs each:

| Binary | Mean | Range |
|---|---|---|
| same install without a Cargo workspace (floor) | 79 ms | 74 to 88 ms |
| `main` | 1.94 s | 1.70 to 2.43 s |
| this PR before the fix (re-hashing every slot file against the store) | 19.1 s | 8.7 to 27.4 s |
| this PR | 174 ms | 167 to 203 ms |

`pnpm install --offline --force` takes 1.89 s with this PR and 2.10 s on `main`. After the warm install, `cargo fetch --offline` verifies every vendored crate against its `.cargo-checksum.json`, and a slot whose marker is deleted is re-materialized by the next install.

## Squash Commit Body

```text
A repeat install in a Cargo workspace re-ran the full materialize pipeline
for every crate in Cargo.lock even when every crate was already in the
store: a store-index lookup and integrity check per crate, a regenerated
.cargo-checksum.json, and a forced re-import of the slot. On a 774-crate
workspace that was about 2.6 s of a 3.6 s no-op install.

download_crates now partitions the locked crates by probing each store
slot for its completion marker before opening the store index or asking
the registry for its configuration. import_indexed_dir places
.cargo-checksum.json last, so a slot whose manifest names the lockfile's
checksum is a finished import and is linked as it is; the remaining
crates take the download-and-import path as before. The registry
configuration is fetched only for those, so an offline repeat install
with a warm store asks the registry for nothing. config.force disables
the skip, matching the force semantics of the npm warm-slot probe.

The slot is a store directory and is trusted once complete, the way a
global virtual store slot is: verifyStoreIntegrity covers the store files
an import reads, and its documentation already states that it detects
accidental corruption rather than a writable store. Re-hashing every slot
file against the store on each install would have cost more than the
materialization it replaces.

The checksum manifest is now an explicit marker in marker_file. It was
the marker only by sorting first among a crate's files, which a crate
shipping .appveyor.yml or a similar dotfile breaks, so an interrupted
import of such a crate could have left a slot that looked finished. The
git vendoring path, which already probed the manifest, shares the probe.

Closes pnpm/tasks#69.
```

## Checklist

- [x] I checked the referenced issue and verified that none of the PRs
  already linked to it solves it.
- [x] New features are implemented only in the Rust pnpm v12 CLI. Bug fixes
  are implemented in every affected version.
- [x] Added a changeset (`pnpm changeset`) if this PR changes any published
  package. Keep it short and written for pnpm users — it becomes a release note.
- [x] Added or updated tests.
- [x] Updated the documentation if needed.

---
Written by an agent (Claude Code, claude-fable-5-1).

pullRequest.title: fix(python): Raise on String operands in eager Series true division
pullRequest.body:
Another drive-by that 🤖 Claude noticed when working on https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/30018.

Lazy mode already rejects String in true division. However, in eager mode, `Series.__truediv__` and `Series.__rtruediv__` silently parsed strings as numerics prior to delegating to the Rust kernels. This created a mismatch between the lazy mode and eager mode, when both should have matching behavior. In this situation, the division should not happen if any of the operands is a String type. 

The example I used:

```python
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series(["4"])
f = pl.Series([2.0], dtype=pl.Float32)
cases = [
    ("s / f", lambda: s / f), ("f / s", lambda: f / s), ('f / "4"', lambda: f / "4"),
    ('"4" / f', lambda: "4" / f), ("2.0 / s", lambda: 2.0 / s), ('"4" / s', lambda: "4" / s),
]
for name, fn in cases:
    try:
        print(name, "->", fn().to_list())
    except Exception as e:
        print(name, "->", type(e).__name__ + ":", e)
```

Before:

```
s / f -> [2.0]
f / s -> InvalidOperationError: div operation not supported for dtypes `str` and `str`
f / "4" -> [0.5]
"4" / f -> [2.0]
2.0 / s -> [0.5]
"4" / s -> [1.0]
```

After:

```
s / f -> InvalidOperationError: division with 'String' datatypes is not allowed
f / s -> InvalidOperationError: division with 'String' datatypes is not allowed
f / "4" -> InvalidOperationError: division with 'String' datatypes is not allowed
"4" / f -> InvalidOperationError: division with 'String' datatypes is not allowed
2.0 / s -> InvalidOperationError: division with 'String' datatypes is not allowed
"4" / s -> InvalidOperationError: division with 'String' datatypes is not allowed
```

🤖 Claude Opus 5.5 for finding the fix and writing the tests. I wrote the fix, while also verifying the tests and logic.

pullRequest.title: [AI, graph indexing variations] Graph builder cleanups before indexing variations
pullRequest.body:
First part of the HNSW index construction variations: https://app.notion.com/p/qdrant/Indexing-algorithm-s-variation-design-doc-3f4674779d3380d2ac7ecb7825ca9940

Two small changes to the HNSW build, split out of the graph builder work that follows in the next PRs of this stack.

- `GpuInsertContext` no longer borrows `GpuVectorStorage`. It holds an `Arc` of it and has no lifetime, so one struct can own both the uploaded vectors and the insert context for payload blocks. The GPU graph builder needs this.
- `build_additional_links` no longer counts the points it links. Since the GPU integration (#5535), the number of indexed points is every non-deleted point, also when `m == 0`, and the points of payload blocks are a subset of them. So `indexed_vectors.max(indexed_payload_vectors)` never changed the result, and `indexed_vector_count` stays the number of non-deleted points.

No behavior changes.

pullRequest.title: fix(CI): flaky tests and retry merge queue tests with backoff
pullRequest.body:
### Description

Adds retries to the merge queue test runs and fixes the most common flaky tests from the last two months of CI.

**Retries.** Unit tests, `make test-all` and coverage now use the nextest `ci` profile:
- Failing tests are retried twice, with a 1–4s backoff. Retries used to run back to back without backoff which didn't help.
- The run continues after a failure. `make test-all` used to stop at the first one. This means if multiple tests fail in make test-all all the failures will be reported instead of just one
- A single test running for more than 10 minutes is killed and retried, instead of running until the job times out.

**Flaky test fixes.** All test-side; mostly tests not waiting long enough or waiting on the wrong thing.

| Test | Cause | CI jobs affected (Aug–Sep) |
|---|---|---|
| Kafka tests | used a topic before Kafka finished creating it (the 09-30 failure) | 13 |
| `test_ingest_v1_happy_path` | ingested into a new index before it was ready, got a 404 | 13 |
| `test_ingester_close_shards` | held a lock the code under test also needed | 4 |
| retiring-indexer / graceful-shutdown tests | exact doc counts fail if a document is written twice, which ingest v2 allows | 2 |
| `test_indexer_exceeding_max_num_partitions` | the test's fast-forwarded clock could skip past a timeout | 1 |

### How was this PR tested?

`make test-all` passes, and clippy and fmt are clean.

Each fixed test was run repeatedly on an overloaded machine with retries off, before and after the fix:

| Tests | Failed runs before | Failed runs after |
|---|---|---|
| Kafka tests | 2 of 30 | 0 of 30 |
| `test_ingester_close_shards` | 2 of 300 | 0 of 300 |
| `test_indexer_exceeding_max_num_partitions` | 2 of 200 | 0 of 200 |
| Retiring-indexer and graceful-shutdown tests | 4 of 20 | 0 of 120 |
| `test_retiring_indexer_receives_empty_plan` crash | 1 in 3 full-suite runs | 0 of 60 |
| Janitor delete and garbage-collection tests | 5 of 200 | 0 of 200 |
| Health-check tests (heavier load) | 21 of 30 | 0 of 30 |

pullRequest.title: Clarify `in_place_scope` docs on thread-pool selection
pullRequest.body: Clarifies #1165. Tasks spawned through the scope handle use the scope's pool. Ambient Rayon operations inside the closure, including free join, free spawn, and parallel iterators, do not inherit that pool: they use the caller's current worker pool or the global pool when the caller is outside Rayon. Explicit ThreadPool operations select their own pool. Applies equally to in_place_scope_fifo. Docs-only; no behavior change.

pullRequest.title: docs: add v0.11.10 changelog
Print full anyhow context in re_mcap and re_ros_msg errors
pullRequest.body:
### Related

* Part of #8681

### What

An error that wraps an `anyhow::Error` was only printing the outermost context, so the actual cause got lost for whoever has to debug it. #12882 fixed most of these, but two call sites still flattened the chain: `re_mcap::Error::Other`, which regressed to `#[error(transparent)]` when the crate moved to `crates/data_flow/`, and `re_ros_msg`'s `CdrDecodeError::Message`.

Both now use the alternate form `{0:#}`, which walks the source chain, so errors read as `outer context: root cause` instead of `outer context`. This is the same pattern #12882 used for `Other(#[from] anyhow::Error)`.

### Testing

`cargo test -p re_mcap -p re_ros_msg --all-features` passes.

### Review

Mostly the code. Two things worth a second look:

* Changing `Other` from `#[error(transparent)]` to `#[error("{0:#}")]` stops forwarding `source()`. #12882 already made that same trade for this variant, so I kept it consistent.
* I checked every `anyhow::Error`-wrapping variant in the repo; these were the last two that flattened the chain.

### Agent

Drafted with AI assistance; a human reviewed every line and ran the tests. Confidence: high for this change. It is a two-line behavior restore that matches the merged precedent in #12882, and I verified that no remaining `#[error(transparent)]` sits over an `anyhow::Error` anywhere in the workspace.

pullRequest.title: Keep watching the config file across symlink swaps
pullRequest.body:
Kubernetes updates a mounted ConfigMap by writing a new timestamped directory, re-pointing the `..data` symlink and deleting the old directory; `config.toml` itself is a symlink through `..data`. Two things in the server broke on that:

- `restate-server` canonicalized `--config-file` at startup, so the loader's path was the timestamped directory. After the swap that directory is gone and the reload failed with `No such file or directory`.
- On the remove event the loader re-armed the watch on the event's path, the same dead directory, so nothing was watched afterwards and later updates went unnoticed.

The path is now kept as given (`std::path::absolute`, so it still survives the base-dir chdir) and the configured path is re-watched after a remove. The regression test reproduces the kubelet swap twice; it is Linux-only because FSEvents on macOS delivers no event for this pattern.

Observed on kind before the fix: first update → `Error updating configuration, config was not updated: No such file or directory ... in config/..2026_10_16_18_05_22.2867132780/config.toml`, second update never detected. After the fix: both updates applied, pod untouched.

pullRequest.title: Use checked arithmetic in Arena::with_capacity
pullRequest.body:
`with_capacity` uses `next_power_of_two()` which can wrap to 0 in release mode for very large inputs. This could cause `Block::alloc` to receive a size smaller than `size_of::<Block>()`, resulting in an undersized write and UB.

Switched to `checked_add` + `checked_next_power_of_two` so it panics instead of wrapping.
Happy to adjust if you'd prefer a different approach.

pullRequest.title: web: Avoid a reference cycle in audio buffer callbacks
pullRequest.body:
## Description

Each audio `Buffer` owns its `onended` closure, which strongly captures the same buffer. This cycle prevents buffer cleanup when the audio backend is dropped.

Capture a `Weak` reference instead. `WebAudioBackend.buffers` keeps the buffers alive during playback, and each callback temporarily upgrades the reference to refill the buffer.

## Testing

No new automated test is included. Exercising the real buffer lifecycle requires a browser; the ownership relationship is documented beside the callback.

pullRequest.title: feat(build-std): Add build.build-std.when and crates config keys
pullRequest.body:
### What does this PR try to resolve?

As part of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/155363 this PR adds the new build-std UI config keys specified in the [`build-std=always`](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3874-build-std-always.html#proposal) RFC. The keys currently don't do anything, but their behaviour will be gated on an unstable `-Z` flag in a later patch.

Not explicitly mentioned in the RFC is the perma-unstable ability to supply a custom list of crates to `build.build-std.crates`. However `-Zbuild-std` already allows custom crate names, so this addition allows parity with that flag [Explicit builtin dependencies
](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3875-build-std-explicit-dependencies.html#why-unstably-allow-all-names-for-builtin-crates) will allow any name of crate for builtins under a perma-unstable feature so I feel this feature does not add a significant maintenance burden to Cargo.

The plan is to use the new config keys to unblock merging of implicit builtin dependencies to enable build-std to work with explicit builtin dependencies. At some point in the future `-Zbuild-std` will be removed and these keys will replace it.

### How to test and review this PR?

Commit by commit - all commits pass tests and rustfmt.

pullRequest.title: Map `*-windows-gnullvm` targets to `*-windows-gnu` for clang
pullRequest.body:
Clang doesn't know the `gnullvm` environment: `--target=x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm` fails with `error: version 'llvm' in target triple 'x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm' is invalid`. When a build script cross-compiles to a gnullvm target, `find_effective_target` takes `TARGET` and passes it to libclang unchanged, so binding generation fails. Native gnullvm builds aren't affected because no `--target` is added when host and target match.

The gnullvm targets use the same clang triple as their gnu counterparts (rustc's own `llvm-target` for them is `*-pc-windows-gnu`, and cc-rs maps them the same way), so `rust_to_clang_target` now rewrites the environment the way it already does for Apple, RISC-V and ESP-IDF targets.

pullRequest.title: Fix statement comment wrapping
pullRequest.body:
- Rename `line_start` to `comment_prefix`

    This naming was a bit confusing: I would expect a 'line start' of a
    comment to include any leading indent etc., e.g. for the comments in:

        // top level comment

        fn f() {
            // function comment
            ...
        }

    I would expect:

    * `line_start`: `// `, and
    * `line_start`: `    // `

    Rather than both to be `// `.

- Fix comments not taking full width when combined

    By excluding the width of the indent when combining comments, since
    `last_line_width` includes this. Otherwise e.g. when formatting:

        V------V (indent)    (end of line) ---V
                // some comment with final word
                // new line fits word

    We'd would compute the offset using:

        last_line_width = "        // word".len()`

    (i.e. indent+comment prefix+content), then subtract only the width of
    the comment prefix (and `" "`) and incorrectly conclude that won't fit
    if combined with the following comment.

    References: rust-lang/rustfmt#7167

- [x] I did not use an LLM to create a change in this PR.
- [ ] I used an LLM to create a change in this PR, and I have explained below how it was used.

pullRequest.title: fix(heal): decide object absence from storage evidence, not source
pullRequest.body:
## Related Issues

Implements rustfs/backlog#2900 (S02a of rustfs/backlog#2872). Fixes #8132. Ends the resubmission loop reported in #7997, #8235 and #5950: a heal task that finds an object absent is no longer reported as `recreate_failed`, and a best-effort producer can no longer requeue the same absent or terminally failed object on every tick.

## Summary of Changes

**One classifier instead of five.** `classify_heal_error` in `crates/heal/src/error.rs` returns a `HealErrorClass` (`Absent`, `Transient`, `LockContention`, `DanglingGrace`, `NoHealRequired`, `Aborted`, `Permanent`) from typed variants. The five sites that used to classify independently now adapt that one result: the erasure-set healer's `classify_heal_object_error` (per-object action mapping), the task-level `is_missing_object_dir_heal_result`, `is_transient_lock_or_timeout_error` and `is_no_heal_required_error`, the `error.rs` recovery predicates (`is_recoverable_heal`, `is_recoverable_object_heal`, `is_dangling_delete_grace`), and the storage adapter's existence-check matcher. `is_object_level_not_found_error` and `is_object_not_found_heal_error` are deleted. Every input on which the old sites disagreed has a regression (`Error::Disk(FileNotFound)` was Failed in the healer but absent in the task; `Disk(VolumeNotFound)` was unrecoverable while `Storage(VolumeNotFound)` was recoverable; typed `ObjectNotFound` was not an object-dir not-found; wrapped transient errors were Failed in the healer).

**Absence is decided by evidence.** An object-level not-found returned by the locked storage heal (ecstore returns `FileNotFound` only when every disk in the quorum read answered NotFound) is `Absent` for every request source and every `recreate_missing` value. `heal_object` no longer branches on `recreate_missing` or on the source when the unlocked existence check misses: it always runs the locked storage heal and classifies its result. `recreate_missing_object` is deleted; a recreate from parity happens only on the durable MRF path, which carries the write anchor and its own absence-proof receipt (unchanged). The `recreate_missing` request field is still parsed and forwarded to storage, where it only controls bucket-volume recreation; the read-repair producer in `crates/ecstore/src/set_disk/core/io_primitives.rs` stops forcing it to `Some(true)`.

**Two whitelists removed.** `skip_missing_usage_observation` (#8135) and `skip_scanner_synthetic_object_dir_missing` (#3839) were special cases of the general rule and are gone; their tests are rewritten as general-rule cases in `crates/heal/src/heal/task/tests/absent_verdict.rs` and `tests/usage_observation.rs`.

**Display text only at the boundary.** The heal crate no longer matches error text except in `classify_error_display`, which maps the canonical typed displays of old peers and known type wrappers back to a class (contention and transient needles win over absence phrases, so a transient failure can never be misread as absence). Contextual task messages containing object names do not establish absence. It carries `RUSTFS_COMPAT_TODO(backlog-2900-heal-error-display)` and a register entry. Inventory before this change: 11 non-test `contains(` sites in the heal crate (`error.rs` 1, `task.rs` 10) plus the needle list in `storage.rs`; after: the boundary function only (the four sites in `heal/resume/replacement.rs` belong to backlog#2902).

**Per-object disposition memory.** `crates/heal/src/heal/manager/disposition.rs` adds a node-local `HealDispositionCache` keyed by `(bucket, object, version, pool, set)` with values `Absent`, `RetryExhausted` or `Permanent` plus count, timestamp and the producing task id. It is bounded (100,000 entries, least-recently-used eviction), expiring (24 h), and consulted exactly once per submission, before `admit_request_to_queue`, for `HealType::Object` requests that are not administrator starts, not forced, not above normal priority, not dry runs and carry no durable MRF anchor. `Absent` hits are dropped until expiry; `RetryExhausted`/`Permanent` hits re-admit on an exponential schedule (1 min doubling, capped at 1 h). A dropped request receives `Dropped(PolicyDropped)` with the task id that produced the verdict and is counted under `rustfs_heal_admission_total{context="disposition_cache"}`. The scheduler records the verdict when a task reaches a terminal result and clears the key after a positive completion. Recording, admission and clearing use the same pool/set selector, so a late absence result from an old pool cannot suppress repair in another pool or an unscoped request. The memory is not a receipt, never releases a durable responsibility, and starts empty after a restart (documented in `docs/architecture/placement-repair-invariants.md`). Metrics: `rustfs_heal_disposition_cache_hits_total{disposition}` and `rustfs_heal_disposition_cache_entries`.

**Not changed (fences kept).** ecstore's absence-proof conditions, the durable MRF responsibility release rules, the `AuthoritativelyAbsent` receipt path, priority mapping, the queue dedup key semantics, and `heal/resume/*`, `manager/root_recovery.rs`, `manager/unclean_shutdown.rs` (owned by backlog#2902). `HealAdmissionResult` keeps its wire shape; a dedicated drop reason would change `crates/heal-contracts` and the `heal_control` wire enum and is left to the owner's decision.

## Verification

Follow-up fix `e3f124bbaed04b06fea30641bb75435634bb8c46`:

- Three new regression tests failed before the fix: cross-scope admission, an unhealthy admin heal whose object name contains `File not found`, and contextual absence text classification.
- `cargo nextest run -p rustfs-heal --lib --no-fail-fast -E 'test(classify) | test(disposition) | test(absent) | test(not_found) | test(recreate) | test(read_repair)'`: 71 passed, including all three regressions. Built with `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` and two build jobs.
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `git diff --check`, `./scripts/check_doc_paths.sh`, and `./scripts/check_architecture_migration_rules.sh`: passed.
- No local full-workspace or cluster e2e run for this follow-up; CI is being monitored.

Original implementation validation:

Tested commit: `8e68ca8021c75bd32490da3cda9fda8c8d16c65f` on top of `ab7001a714c912100f0c01740c271aa58296784c` (origin/main), no local changes beyond this diff. Build environment: shared target directory, `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`, stable toolchain.

- Failing before / passing after: `cargo nextest run -p rustfs-heal --lib --no-fail-fast -E 'test(classify) | test(not_found) | test(recreate) | test(absent) | test(disposition) | test(read_repair)'` on the base code at the first commit of this branch: 58 run, 45 passed, 13 failed, exit 100 (the 13 are the regressions for the inconsistencies above); after the fix: 72 run, 72 passed (filter extended with `test(canonicalize)` for the rewritten admin object-dir case).
- `cargo nextest run -p rustfs-heal --lib --no-fail-fast`: 814 run, 814 passed (1 leaky), 1 skipped.
- `cargo nextest run -p rustfs-heal --test heal_concurrent_delete_test --test mrf_pipeline_test --test usage_observation_read_repair_test`: 23 run, 23 passed (1 leaky).
- `cargo clippy -p rustfs-heal --lib --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings`: clean (exit 0; only the pre-existing macOS linker `__eh_frame` note).
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `git diff --check`, `./scripts/check_logging_guardrails.sh`, `./scripts/check_doc_paths.sh`, `./scripts/check_architecture_migration_rules.sh`: passed.

Not run: `make pre-pr`, workspace-wide tests, and clippy for `rustfs-ecstore` (the ecstore change removes one assignment; the crate compiled as a dependency of the heal tests). The S00 protection gates (G-EXP / G-REB / G-DEC) are not delivered yet and were not executed.

## Impact

- Behavior: a heal for a deleted object completes instead of failing, for every source; the `recreate_failed` ERROR pair and the `task_failed` ERROR for absent objects disappear. The task's progress counts the absent target as one scanned, one skipped object (the accounting the usage-observation skip already used), and its outcome stays `Unknown` because no absence proof is claimed. Best-effort resubmissions of an absent object within 24 h on the same node are answered from memory with `Dropped(PolicyDropped)` (new admission `context` label `disposition_cache`); terminally failing objects are retried on a backoff instead of on every producer tick.
- Known limitation: an unversioned key that is deleted and re-created within the TTL on the same node and pool/set scope defers background heal admission for that key by up to the TTL; foreground reads, administrator heals, high-priority candidates and durable MRF repairs are unaffected.
- Compatibility: no wire, persisted format, configuration or environment-variable changes. `rustfs-heal` drops its unused `rustfs-data-usage` dependency.
- Documentation: `docs/architecture/placement-repair-invariants.md` (new "Per-object disposition memory" section), `docs/architecture/compat-cleanup-register.md` (new entry).

## Additional Notes

Integration with #8700 (backlog#2902): that PR adds `StorageError::DeleteRecoveryLegacyAmbiguous` and asserts it is not a retryable heal error. Under this classifier the variant reaches the display boundary and classifies `Permanent`, so the two changes compose as they are; whichever PR merges second rebases and adds an explicit `DeleteRecoveryLegacyAmbiguous => Permanent` arm in `classify_storage_error` so the verdict does not depend on the fallback.

Review shape (two sequential passes, correctness/coverage then concurrency/compatibility/security/performance). Pass one found and fixed an unused `EcstoreError` import left by the removed predicates, the now-unused `rustfs-data-usage` dependency, and one old test that asserted the `recreate_failed` failure for an administrator object-dir target (rewritten to assert the real invariant: the key is not canonicalized). Pass two: the cache mutex is a leaf lock taken without awaiting while held; admission takes it under the existing active/queue/retrying lock order, the scheduler takes it before re-acquiring the active-heals lock. Worst-case memory at the default bound is on the order of tens of MB of key strings. Erasure-set healer verdicts widened from Failed to Transient only for wrapper variants that the task-level predicates already treated as recoverable.


Follow-up review used two sequential passes. Correctness and coverage: scoped absence cannot cross pool/set selectors, and object-name text cannot become an absence verdict; the new tests failed before the fix and pass afterward. Simplicity: both changes stay in the existing key and classifier. Security: contextual object names are excluded from absence parsing. Concurrency/durability: no lock ordering, receipt or persistence changes. Compatibility: canonical legacy errors and nested type wrappers still work; contextual messages fail closed. Performance: cache capacity and expiry are unchanged, with two optional indices added per key and bounded prefix stripping.

## Motivation
Native duplication currently resets carets to the beginning of the copied block and clears selections. Subsequent typing therefore loses the original editing position or selected text.

## Changes
- Preserve each caret's relative byte offset and each selection's text and orientation on its corresponding copy.
- Add `duplicate_line_above` through the existing native action and command infrastructure, with labels in all 15 locales. No new default shortcut.
- Preserve existing native grouped undo/redo; no new transaction API or plugin-wrapper changes.
- Cover UTF-8, CRLF, EOF without a newline, selection endpoints at the next line's start, and shared/overlapping copied blocks. Remove obsolete tests that pinned the old reset behavior.

## Verification
- `cargo test -p fresh-editor --test all_tests duplicate_line -- --nocapture`: 16 passed; one pre-existing ignored showcase.
- Native keyboard/palette smoke: duplicate above, type on the copied text, save, and undo typing and duplication back to the original file.

pullRequest.title: fix: reject zero SMOL_THREADS value
pullRequest.body:
SMOL_THREADS=0 creates a range `1..=0` which yields no worker threads, causing tasks spawned with `smol::spawn` to hang forever.

Non-numeric values already fall back to 1 because `parse::<usize>` fails, but `0` parsed successfully and produced an empty range.

Add `.filter(|&n| n > 0)` so that a zero value falls back to the default of 1, matching the behavior for invalid values.

Closes #381

pullRequest.title: feat(format): add expanded VALUES row layout
pullRequest.body:
## What kind of change does this PR introduce?

Formatter feature and bug fix, with configuration, generated bindings, and documentation updates.

## What is the current behavior?

`VALUES` rows stay on one line when they fit within `lineWidth`. There is no option to put every tuple on its own indented line. Separators between tuples always use trailing commas, even with `commaStyle: "leading"`.

Related: [#816](https://github.com/supabase-community/postgres-language-server/pull/816) introduced leading commas for fill lists; this change applies that behavior to `VALUES` rows.

## What is the new behavior?

Add `valuesRowLayout: "expanded"` (CLI: `--values-row-layout expanded`) to put each `VALUES` tuple on its own indented line. The default remains `"fit"`.

With expanded rows and leading commas:

```sql
values
  ('MONTHLY', 1)
  , ('QUARTERLY', 3)
  , ('HALF_YEAR', 6);
```

- Honor `commaStyle` between tuples in both layouts, using the shared comma-separated list helper.
- Keep short tuples compact and allow long tuples to wrap within `lineWidth`.
- Apply the option to `INSERT`, standalone `VALUES`, subqueries, and CTEs.
- Expose the option in the JSON schema, TypeScript bindings, CLI reference, and formatting documentation.

## Additional context

- Regression tests cover both comma styles, tabs, a single row, long tuples, nested statements, comments, and idempotence.
- Formatter, configuration, and CLI formatting tests pass, as does `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features`.
- All PR CI checks pass, including Linux, macOS, Windows, WASM, generated files, and JavaScript packages.

pullRequest.title: Fix concurrent index conflicts and batch full-text indexing
pullRequest.body:
Thank you for submitting this pull request. We really appreciate you spending the time to work on SurrealDB. 🚀 🎉

Before proceeding, please add any of the following labels that apply:

* `breaking-change` if this PR includes a breaking change. This label is not needed for bug fixes, which change output in line with a user's original expectations.
* `needs-documentation` if documentation is needed to explain the change made in the PR.
* `Modifies env vars or commands` if any changes are made to environment variables or command flags.

## What is the motivation?

Concurrent index building can fail or degrade badly when records are modified while the builder is scanning the table or draining pending index updates.

The conflict risk comes from three behaviours:

1. The initial-build write transaction read `!ip` / `!ig` queue handoff records. Those records are written by concurrent user transactions while the initial build scans the table, so the initial-build write transaction could see optimistic read/write conflicts even though initial indexing should stay conflict-free and fail-fast.
2. `maybe_consume` could still write `!ip` keys after the initial build phase because `initial_build_complete` used relaxed ordering. The appending phase deletes those same `!ip` keys, so stale phase visibility can create write-write conflicts.
3. `index_appending_range` and the following `tx.commit()` used `catch!`, so retryable storage conflicts were treated as fatal build errors instead of being retried.

Full-text concurrent builds also recreated `FullTextIndex` for every document in a batch. That repeatedly reloads analyzer/index state and causes unnecessary overhead as batch size grows.

## What does this change do?

This change keeps the initial build out of active queue handoff contention, makes concurrent index appending resilient to transient transaction conflicts, and reduces full-text indexing overhead.

* Reads initial-build `!ip` / `!ig` handoff records through a separate read-only transaction instead of the initial-build write transaction.
* Reuses one read-only handoff lookup transaction for each initial indexing batch, avoiding a new read transaction per indexed record.
* Keeps initial-build progress publication after the batch commit succeeds, so `initial` status does not advance for an uncommitted batch.
* Keeps legacy primary-appending cleanup outside the initial-build write transaction, with guarded cleanup for the old batch-id-0 sentinel.
* Adds retry handling around appending batch processing and commit. Retryable `TransactionConflict` errors now cancel the current transaction, restore the appending `updated` counter to its pre-attempt value, sleep briefly, rescan the pending keys, and retry.
* Publishes appending progress only after the appending transaction commits and completed queue entries have been cleaned, so `updated` status reflects committed work.
* Changes `initial_build_complete` to an acquire/release phase boundary and flips it while holding the queue lock, so new consumers cannot keep enqueueing `!ip` keys after the builder enters the appending phase.
* Adds reusable full-text helpers to create one `FullTextIndex` per indexing transaction/batch, then reuses it across all records in that batch instead of recreating it per document.
* Moves `BuildingStatus::Indexing` updates out of the per-record loops, preserving the same final `initial`, `pending`, and `updated` values with fewer lock acquisitions.

No public API, SQL syntax, wire format, catalog schema, environment variable, or command flag changes are included.

## What is your testing strategy?

Ran the focused concurrent-index and formatting checks:

```bash
cargo fmt -p surrealdb-core
cargo test -p surrealdb-core index_appending -- --nocapture
cargo test -p surrealdb-core define_statement_index_concurrently_building_status -- --nocapture
cargo test -p surrealdb-core multi_index_concurrent_test_create_update_delete -- --nocapture
git diff --check
```

The concurrent building-status tests cover both standard and full-text concurrent index builds with updates/deletes during indexing. The multi-index stress test covers concurrent create/update/delete workloads across multiple full-text indexes with compaction running. In the latest local run, `index_appending` compiled `surrealdb-core` successfully but matched 0 runnable tests in this package.

## Security Considerations

No direct security implications. This change is limited to background index building, transaction retry handling, status accounting, and full-text index batching. It does not touch authentication, authorization, session handling, namespace/database isolation rules, user-controlled resource limits, or error responses exposed to users.

## Is this related to any issues?

Related to #7274.

pullRequest.title: fix(relayer): reject zero indexer block batch size
pullRequest.body:
## What

- Reject a zero BlockBatchSize in InitFromConfig before opening the database or dialing RPC clients.
- Add a regression test with valid concurrency that verifies initialization fails before OpenDBFunc is called.
- Give the existing zero-concurrency test a valid block batch size to isolate the two checks.

## Why

The indexer accepts --blockBatchSize=0 or BLOCK_BATCH_SIZE=0.

When filter has pending blocks, j += i.blockBatchSize leaves the batch start unchanged, while the batch end and latestIndexedBlockNumber remain at the previous cursor. The resulting range has its start after its end.

RPC failures do not resolve this: event-indexing errors are logged after retries, and the loop continues without advancing.

Rejecting zero during initialization prevents this configuration from reaching the filtering loop.

## Validation

The Linux test shard for #1810 ran 2,291 tests: 2,290 passed and the file-open responsiveness test failed because a frame took 1.452556301 seconds against a 1.436-second threshold derived from a separate synchronous open. pullRequest.title: fix(tauri-runtime-wry): don't panic in undecorated-resizing hit-test when the webview is reparented
pullRequest.body:
### What

The Linux undecorated-resizing hit-test installs `button-press-event` / `touch-event` handlers on the WebKit webview that walk exactly two ancestors and unwrap a downcast to `gtk::Window`:

```rust
// This one should be GtkBox
if let Some(window) = webview.parent().and_then(|w| w.parent()) {
  // Safe to unwrap unless this is not from tao
  let window: gtk::Window = window.downcast().unwrap();
```

The handlers run on **every** left click (the `is_decorated()` check happens after the unwrap), so any application that reparents the webview inside the window — a legitimate thing for an embedder to do, e.g. packing the webview into a `GtkPaned` to dock a native side panel — panics the main thread on the **first click** anywhere in the page:

```
thread 'main' panicked at tauri-runtime-wry-2.11.0/src/undecorated_resizing.rs:546:57:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Widget { inner: TypedObjectRef { inner: 0x…, type: GtkBox } }
```

(With `webview → GtkPaned → GtkBox`, the second ancestor is the `GtkBox`, and the downcast fails.)

### Fix

Resolve the webview's **toplevel** (`WidgetExt::toplevel()`) and downcast it gracefully, in both handlers. For the stock tao hierarchy this resolves to exactly the same window; for reparented hierarchies it finds the correct toplevel at any nesting depth — so undecorated drag-resize keeps working there too, instead of merely not crashing.

### How we hit it

Tauri 2 desktop app (decorated window) that embeds a native VTE terminal beside the webview by moving the webview into a `GtkPaned`. Worked fine on X11 sessions for weeks; on a Wayland session the embed path engaged and every session died on the first click. Repro is deterministic: reparent the webview into any container after window creation, click once.

Patch is identical in both call sites; `cargo check -p tauri-runtime-wry` clean; covector changeset included (`patch:bug`).

pullRequest.title: fix(linux): isolate failure state for each download
pullRequest.body:
## Fix

Move the failure flag into the per-download `connect_download_started` closure. The failed and finished handlers still share state for one download, but cannot affect another download in the same context.

Closes #1892.

Resetting one context-wide flag on each new start would still be incorrect for overlapping downloads; giving each download its own allocation avoids that coupling without changing callback semantics.

## Native verification

Reproduced with Wry 0.57.0 via Tauri 2.12.3 on Ubuntu 24.04 / WebKitGTK:

- Start a blob export whose destination handler returns `false`: canceled download reports failure.
- Correct the destination configuration and export again without restarting.
- Before this fix: second file has the complete expected 433-byte content, but completion reports `path=None, success=false`.
- With this exact source patch applied through a command-local Cargo path override: the first download still reports failure; the next Markdown export reports its actual path and `success=true`, and a subsequent JSON export does too (830 bytes). UI names those paths. Same app process throughout failure → recovery.

The native application used a production frontend and a real released sidecar, in an isolated network/PID namespace with a fresh HOME; no provider keys, inference or synthetic completion callbacks. The original released application and global Cargo registry were not modified.

`cargo fmt --all -- --check` passed (stable rustfmt prints the existing nightly-only `imports_granularity` warnings). The full Tauri consumer native build passed with the path-patched Wry. Overlapping native transfers were not separately exercised; their isolation follows from per-download allocation and the unchanged callback captures.

### What is changed and how it works?

Issue Number: Ref #19615

Port #20179 (commit f853b1959d8e21939a3a2b84031cfd2d9553b2c2) to `feature/release-8.5-materialized-view`.

pullRequest.title: boards: linker script: remove redundant ENTRY directive
pullRequest.body:
Tock's canonical entry point is called `initialize_ram_jump_to_main`, which is set using the `ENTRY` directive earlier in the linker script. This overrides a redundant `ENTRY` directive that was presumably left in the file accidentally.

It seems like we haven't noticed this as, if `_start` isn't defined, the linker silently falls back onto the start of `.text` and, for LLVM-LLD, it respects the _first_ `ENTRY` directive. Unfortunately, GNU LD diverges from this and respects the _last_ `ENTRY` directive.

pullRequest.title: Mark EVFILT_USER Waker events readable on NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonFly
pullRequest.body:
Fixes #2026

### What

On NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonFly BSD, events produced by `Waker::wake` are no longer readable: `Event::is_readable()` returns `false`. The `Waker` docs promise readable readiness, and event loops that only act on readable events miss the wakeup.

### Why

d07b022 and 8fe57d7 (released in v1.2.3) switched these platforms from the pipe waker to the `EVFILT_USER` based waker. `event::is_readable` in `src/sys/unix/selector/kqueue.rs` was not updated: its `cfg` only treats `filter == EVFILT_USER` as readable on FreeBSD and the Apple targets, so on the three switched platforms the `not(...)` branch returns `false`.

### Small example

```rust
let waker = Waker::new(poll.registry(), WAKE)?;
waker.wake()?;
poll.poll(&mut events, None)?;
let event = events.iter().next().unwrap();
assert!(event.is_readable()); // fails on NetBSD/OpenBSD/DragonFly since v1.2.3
```

### Why the existing tests missed it

`tests/waker.rs` (line 160) and `tests/regressions.rs` `issue_1205` already assert this, but CI only runs `cargo check`/`build` for netbsd, openbsd and dragonfly. FreeBSD is the only BSD whose tests run in a VM.

### Fix

Add `dragonfly`, `netbsd` and `openbsd` to both `cfg` lists in `event::is_readable` (+6 lines, no other changes).

### Tests

These run the existing tests (`cargo test --all-features --test waker --test regressions`) in VMs (vmactions) on the `breken-ai` fork. The proof workflow lives only on the proof branches and is not part of this PR.

| platform | base (red) | this fix (green) |
|---|---|---|
| NetBSD, OpenBSD @ master 9b4366c | [run 37705825002](https://github.com/breken-ai/mio/actions/runs/37705825002): `issue_1205 ... FAILED` / `assertion failed: waker_event.is_readable()` | [run 37705824998](https://github.com/breken-ai/mio/actions/runs/37705824998): `issue_1205 ... ok`, waker 7/7 ok |
| DragonFly @ v1.2.3 | [run 36683764296](https://github.com/breken-ai/mio/actions/runs/36683764296): `issue_1205 ... FAILED` | [run 36683764575](https://github.com/breken-ai/mio/actions/runs/36683764575): all ok |
| NetBSD full suite @ v1.2.3 | [run 36684117742](https://github.com/breken-ai/mio/actions/runs/36684117742): `waker`, `waker_multiple_wakeups_*`, `waker_wakeup_different_thread` FAILED at `tests/waker.rs:160` | (above) |

(`is_readable` is unchanged between v1.2.3 and master.) The new DragonFly runs on master failed at build time because of a `TMPDIR` setting in my proof workflow, so the DragonFly evidence comes from the v1.2.3 runs above.

Locally, on macOS (kqueue), the waker and regression tests pass, and `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `git diff --check` are clean. macOS already treated `EVFILT_USER` as readable, so the bug can't be reproduced on the host. The BSD proof is fork VM CI only.

### Other affected paths

None found. `setup_waker` and `wake` already cover these platforms. The illumos `event_ports` selector has its own `is_readable`, which this PR does not touch.

### AI disclosure

An AI agent (Claude Code, operating the `breken-ai` account) found this bug, wrote the fix and ran the checks above. The red/green results are from the linked CI runs on real NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonFly VMs. The commit carries an `Assisted-By:` trailer.

pullRequest.title: fix(serve): bind before showing addresses and opening the browser
pullRequest.body:
`trunk serve --open` prints the listening URLs and opens the browser even when the server cannot bind. With the port already taken it opens a tab, then logs `Address already in use`.

`axum_server::bind*()` binds lazily inside `.serve()`, so the failure only surfaces once the spawned task is polled, long after `run()` has called `open::that`.

This binds a `std::net::TcpListener` per address in `spawn_server` before `show_listening`, and passes the listeners to `run_server`, which now uses `from_tcp` / `from_tcp_rustls` instead of `bind` / `bind_rustls`. A bind error propagates out of `spawn_server`, so the existing `?` in `run()` already prevents the browser from opening; no new condition was needed there.

axum-server 0.8 has no `from_tcp_openssl`, so the native-tls path builds the equivalent from `from_tcp` plus `OpenSSLAcceptor`, the same way `from_tcp_rustls` does internally. All three paths bind eagerly; none is left on the lazy path.

Binding up front would make a single unavailable address fatal, which would be a regression: the address list is auto-populated with every loopback interface when none is configured, so a default `trunk serve` would fail on a host where one loopback family is occupied. So a failed bind warns and the server carries on with the rest, erroring only if nothing binds at all. `show_listening` now receives the addresses actually bound, taken from `local_addr()`, which also makes `--port 0` print the resolved port instead of `0`.

Fixes #946

## Verification

- `cargo build`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` all pass
- Feature paths compile: default (rustls), `--no-default-features`, `rustls-aws-lc`, and `native-tls,vendored`
- Only address occupied: warns, then `failed to bind to any of the requested addresses`, prints no URLs, opens no browser
- `[::1]` occupied and `127.0.0.1` free: warns about `[::1]`, prints only the `127.0.0.1` URL, keeps serving (`curl` returns 200)
- `--port 0`: prints the resolved ephemeral port

#988 took the same approach and stalled on the belief that native-tls had no listener-based constructor. That is correct for `from_tcp_openssl`, but the acceptor can be attached to `from_tcp` directly, which closes that gap.

pullRequest.title: postgres: rewrite array subqueries in the frontend
pullRequest.body:
## Description

Restart this draft as a PostgreSQL-only AST rewrite for `ARRAY(query)`. Remove the earlier native array-subquery expression, subquery type, result destination, and related engine changes. Core and the SQLite parser are unchanged relative to the original comparison base.

The PG translator produces an ordinary scalar subquery. Its internal Turso AST has this SQL shape:

```sql
(
    WITH _turso_array_rows(_turso_array_value) AS MATERIALIZED (
        <original query>
    )
    SELECT coalesce(array_agg(_turso_array_value), array())
    FROM _turso_array_rows
)
```

The existing `array()` function constructs the empty array. The original query stays intact, including its WITH clause, ordering, limits, DISTINCT, grouping, windows, VALUES, and compound operations. The CTE's explicit column list names the single result without changing projection aliases, and the generated table name avoids names present in the input query. Keeping the wrapper inside the scalar subquery preserves ordinary outer-column references.

Materialization uses additional temporary storage so collection consumes the original query's completed row sequence. This draft does not introduce a new core query consumer or array-building primitive.

The rewrite provides row collection, not complete PostgreSQL array semantics. Known limitations remain visible:

- Referencing an outer aggregate from the array query fails with `misuse of aggregate function sum()`. Support for this case is deferred for now.
- Ordinary scalar subqueries format array values as text. `(ARRAY(SELECT 17))[1]` consequently returns NULL instead of 17.
- Result metadata reports TEXT (OID 25), not INTEGER[] (OID 1007), for both `ARRAY(SELECT 17)` and its zero-row equivalent.
- Array-valued input is collected as formatted text rather than forming an additional array dimension.
- The rewrite does not add common-type coercion, custom-value representation tracking or normalization, or binary array encoding. It uses the existing array aggregate and type behavior.


## Description of AI Usage

Implemented with Amp at Pedro's request to replace the native implementation with a PG-side rewrite. Amp removed the earlier core changes, exercised the replacement against the unchanged engine, and documented the remaining limitations rather than retaining native fixes that would hide them.

pullRequest.title: Checkpoint before serving imported databases
pullRequest.body:
## Product change and motivation

Finalising an import closed the staged database without a checkpoint, so the reopen replayed every commit since the last periodic checkpoint, all held in memory at once. During an import, that is up to a minute of the heaviest writes, and potentially several GB of memory, all to recover state the database already had.

`DatabaseOpenError::StatisticsPersist` (DBO18) is removed: a statistics persistence failure at startup is now reported as `StatisticsInitialise` (DBO11).

## Implementation

`serve_staged_database` now calls `Database::checkpoint_and_close`, which stops the periodic checkpointer and manually writes a final checkpoint. In case of an error, just print a warning and continue as usual.
Additionally, wrap all the background workers into a single struct for simple `drop` calls.

pullRequest.title: fix(ui): ignore key release events so keys do not fire twice on Windows
pullRequest.body:
## Summary

Fixes #250. On Windows, **every keypress fired twice**, making manual playback control unusable — pressing `Space` to pause immediately resumed playback. `q`, `h`, `l`, `H`, `L`, `p`, `n` and `Esc` were all affected.

## Root cause

crossterm reports **both** a `Press` and a `Release` event for a single physical keypress on Windows (added in crossterm `0.26.0`, "Add key release event for windows"). `handle_event` dispatched every `Event::Key` without checking `KeyEventKind`:

```rust
// src/ui.rs, before
fn handle_event(&mut self, event: Event) {
    self.force_redraw = true;
    if let Event::Key(key) = event {
        self.handle_key_event(key);   // no key.kind check
    }
}
```

So one tap of `Space` ran `toggle_pause()` twice — pause, then instantly resume.

Verified line numbers along the chain:

1. crossterm's Windows parser sets the kind from `key_down` — `crossterm-0.29.0/src/event/sys/windows/parse.rs:286-291` (same for the Alt-code path at `223-228`).
2. crossterm's event source passes it through with no filtering — `crossterm-0.29.0/src/event/source/windows.rs:53`.
3. gitlogue never inspected the kind — searching all 71 `.rs` files for `KeyEventKind` returned zero hits.

Linux and macOS are unaffected, which is why this went unnoticed.

## Fix

Filter on the press at the single dispatch boundary, which covers all keys:

```rust
if key.kind == event::KeyEventKind::Press {
    self.handle_key_event(key);
}
```

`KeyEvent::new()`, used by the existing test helpers, defaults to `KeyEventKind::Press`, so no existing test needed changing.

## Evidence

Drove a real Windows pseudo-console (ConPTY) and sent exactly **one** `p` keystroke to a minimal crossterm harness logging `key.kind`:

```
KEY code=Char('p') kind=Press
KEY code=Char('p') kind=Release     <-- phantom second event for one physical press
```

Differential test — send **one** `Space`, then measure how many bytes the TUI emits in the following second, on two builds from the same tree differing only by the guard:

| Build | Output 1s after a single `Space` | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | **32,803 bytes** | animation keeps running — pause was undone |
| after | **126 bytes** | stays paused |

## Reproduction

```bash
gitlogue --commit HEAD --speed 5
# Press Space once.
# Before: pauses and instantly resumes.
# After:  pauses and stays paused.
```

## Tests

Three regression tests added. All three fail on `main` and pass with the fix:

- `key_release_events_must_not_trigger_a_second_action` — the reported symptom
- `key_release_events_must_not_quit_the_app`
- `key_release_events_must_not_step_an_extra_line`

```
test ui::tests::key_release_events_must_not_quit_the_app ... ok
test ui::tests::key_release_events_must_not_trigger_a_second_action ... ok
test ui::tests::key_release_events_must_not_step_an_extra_line ... ok
```

## CI checks run locally

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` — clean, no warnings
- `cargo test` — **169 passed, 15 failed**; baseline `main` is **166 passed, 15 failed**

The 15 failures are pre-existing and Windows-only (they do not occur on the `ubuntu-22.04` CI runners): `\\?\` extended-length path-prefix mismatches (`src/main.rs:856`), `"Initial console modes not set"` from terminal tests with no attached console (`src/ui.rs:1125`), and config/HOME path-separator assumptions. The failing set is byte-for-byte identical with and without this change, so the patch introduces no new failures.

fix(core): use byte offsets in CJK tokenizer
pullRequest.body:
Closes #423 

## Problem

Indexing or searching Chinese text panics in the lexer:

```text
thread 'sonic-channel-client' (32) panicked at core/src/lexer/token.rs:560:46:
start byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside '维' (bytes 0..3 of string ...)
```

`Tokenizer::tokenize()` fed `jieba_rs::Token::start` — a Unicode (char) offset — into byte slicing in `TokensIter::next()` (`&text_original[start..end]`). Any multi-byte input panics. Full analysis in #423.

## Changes

- `core/src/lexer/token.rs`
  - Chinese path: `token.start` → `token.byte_start` (`jieba_rs::Token::byte_start` is the byte offset in the original input).
  - Japanese path: `token.token_start` → `token.byte_start` (same char-vs-byte confusion; `lindera-tokenizer` 0.31 exposes `byte_start`/`byte_end` as byte positions).
  - Added regression tests:
    - `test_tokenizer_cmn_yields_byte_offsets` — `"我来到北京清华大学"` yields `[(0, "我"), (3, "来到"), (9, "北京"), (15, "清华大学")]`.
    - `test_preprocessor_cmn_tokens_have_valid_ranges` — iterates `Preprocessor::preprocess(text, Some(Lang::Cmn)).tokens()` (the panicking path), asserting `is_char_boundary` and slice-consistent ranges.
- `core/CHANGELOG.md` — entry under `[Unreleased]`.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p sonic-core --lib`: **44 passed, 0 failed** (includes the 2 new tests).
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps --profile lint`: clean.

## Notes

- Branch: `fix/core-cjk-byte-offsets` (from `master`).
- No API changes; only internal offsets corrected. Existing `test_tokenizer_cmn` (words only) still passes.

Release notes

Sourced from @​playwright/test's releases.

v1.64.0

🧰 WebMCP

New page.webmcp and frame.webmcp give access to the tools that a page registers through the experimental WebMCP browser API, so you can test them like any other part of your app:

const browser = await chromium.launch({ args: ['--enable-features=WebMCP'] });
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto('https://example.com');

for (const tool of await page.webmcp.tools())
console.log(tool.name, tool.description);


const result = await page.webmcp.callTool('add', { a: 2, b: 40 });
console.log(result.content[0].text); // "42"

Playwright MCP also supports WebMCP by default, with page-defined tools offered to the agent as webmcp_<tool>. Pass --no-webmcp to opt out.

playwright-cli exposes them as well:

playwright-cli webmcp-list
playwright-cli webmcp-call search_catalog --params '{"query":"cats"}'

🎬 Better videos

Videos can now be recorded at a custom frame rate, and the decorations for actions are styled with plain CSS:

// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

pullRequest.title: fix(pm): enforce package manager option compatibility
pullRequest.body:
## Summary

Reject options that the selected package manager version cannot honor. Older versions can silently ignore these options, including npm versions that attempt to publish despite `--dry-run` and pnpm versions that omit requested JSON output.

- Check command-specific version requirements for npm workspace operations and pnpm build, catalog, pack, and finder options. Keep package names required for `vp why`, including when using `--find-by`.
- Reject npm publish requests using `--dry-run` or `--provenance` when the npm version is unknown, because Vite+ cannot establish that npm will honor those options. Ordinary publish remains available.
- Preserve Yarn Classic script skipping. Use `--skip-builds` for Yarn 2.4 installs and `--mode skip-build` for Yarn 3 and later. Yarn Modern add commands require Yarn 3 or later for script skipping.
- Require Bun 1.4 for production and optional dependency update selection. Remove the older `--omit optional` translation because it excludes installation but still changes optional dependency versions in `package.json`.
- Require Bun 1.4 for recursive and filtered updates in both interactive and noninteractive modes. Vite+ uses one version floor for both modes, even though some older interactive workspace filtering works.

### Version Reference

| Capability | Supported version | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| npm publish `--dry-run` | 5.10.0 stable minimum | [Changelog](https://github.com/npm/npm/blob/v5.10.0/CHANGELOG.md) |
| npm publish `--provenance` | 9.5.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v9.5.0) |
| npm pack workspace selection | 7.9.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v7.9.0) |
| npm publish workspace selection | 7.13.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v7.13.0) |
| npm install, add, remove, update, list, outdated, and explain workspace selection | 7.14.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v7.14.0) |
| npm `--include-workspace-root` | 8.1.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v8.1.0) |
| npm pack `--pack-destination` | 7.18.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v7.18.0) |
| pnpm add `--allow-build` | 10.4.0 | [Changelog](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/v10.4.0/pnpm/CHANGELOG.md#1040) |
| pnpm add `--save-catalog` and `--save-catalog-name` | 10.12.0 | [10.12.1 release notes](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v10.12.1), with the boundary verified against 10.12.0 |
| pnpm recursive and filtered pack | 10.11.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v10.11.0) |
| pnpm list and why `--find-by` | 10.16.0 | [Release notes](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v10.16.0) |
| pnpm publish `--json` | Reject versions from 11.0.0 up to, but excluding, 11.0.7 | [Release notes](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v11.0.7) |

pullRequest.title: Support the sink symbol _ in place of vector operands
pullRequest.body:
PTX allows `_` as a sink in place of a vector operand, e.g. `mov.b64 {_, %r1}, %rd1;` or `ld.global.v4.u32 {_, %r2, _, _}, [%rd1];`. The lexer rejected a lone `_` with a TokenError, which fails the whole module; CuPy's cuRAND PTX uses it heavily.

- The lexer accepts `_` as an identifier.
- When `_` is a destination, identifier resolution declares a fresh register of the operand's type in its place.
- Vector unpack elements get their element type (a `.b64` split in two gives `.b32`).

`_` as a source element (e.g. in a `.v8` store) is still unsupported. Adds `test_ptx!(sink, ...)` (`sink.ptx`, `ll/sink.ll`).

PTX reference, section 9.2: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.4.1/pdf/ptx_isa_9.4.pdf

> For some instructions the destination operand is optional. A bit bucket operand denoted with an un
derscore (_) may be used in place of a destination register.

pullRequest.title: cicd: Remove restore-keys (fallback) to reduce diskspace pressure
pullRequest.body:
# Description

Changes mirrored from https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer-internal/pull/57, description from there:

---
The restore-keys in this format loads all previous target/* artefacts that this specific build step has run. Reason why is because a new update needs exact key match on Cargo.lock hash, and if this is lacking, it will load the most recent artefact. It is unlikely that this previous artefact had a precise hit itself, which means that it too loaded the most recent artefact, etc.

This "cyclical cache restore" plus the lack of any cargo clean, will accumulate the artefact on every single run. For every new build, there will be stale artefacts in target/ which are never cleaned up. Eventually, this accumulation causes diskpressure too large for the nodes to handle. There is also no cargo clean --stale which prunes "dead packages"

Removing this restore-keys will cause a bit of a delay in the pipeline speed, but at the moment none of these jobs are the slowest. So the workflow at large should not be affected

pullRequest.title: docs(resolve): explain resolve.tsConfig.references matching rules
pullRequest.body:
## Motivation

In #16057, a referenced tsconfig placed next to the main tsconfig caught every file under the project root, so the main tsconfig's `paths` were never used and `@src/*` failed to resolve, while `tsc` worked fine. The docs don't explain how Rspack picks a reference, so this layout looks valid to users.

## Changes

- Document the reference matching rules: a reference's base path is its `baseUrl` or its directory; the first reference whose base path contains the importer's directory wins, even without `paths`; the main tsconfig is used only when none match. Matching is directory-based and ignores `include`/`files`/`exclude`.
- Add a warning that putting the main tsconfig and a referenced one, or two referenced ones, in the same directory leads to wrong `paths`, and recommend one tsconfig per directory.

pullRequest.title: fix(runtime): don't block the smol executor in connect_tcp
pullRequest.body:
The smol runtime's `connect_tcp` called the blocking `std::net::TcpStream::connect` inside its async block, so a dial that gets no answer holds the executor thread for the OS connect timeout (135 s on Linux). It now connects through `smol::Async::<TcpStream>::connect`, as the tokio runtime already does.

The new test dials a loopback listener whose accept queue is full and requires a 200 ms timer to win the race. It is Linux-only because it relies on Linux dropping SYNs for a full queue. Without the fix it fails after 135 s; with it, it passes in 0.4 s. `socket2`, already in the tree through `quinn-udp`, becomes a dev-dependency to set the listen backlog, which std cannot do.

This makes the scheduler in the browser environment yield every ~16 ms

#### Concerns

~~- DOM may be partially updated when the browser paints during a yield. This is arguably better than the status quo, where the browser cannot paint at all until the entire batch completes, causing the page to appear frozen.~~

## Description

Adds `cgroup_v2_unified` to the contest suite as `tests/cgroups/unified.rs`, following the layout in #3605. Three tests port runc's `resources.unified` tests from `cgroups.bats` with the same values, and a fourth covers the runtime spec's rule that a key for a controller that is not present is an error:

- every value in `unified` is written to the cgroup file of the same name, including `memory.high`, which no other resource field sets
- `memory.swap.max` is written as given, without the `swap - limit` conversion that the `memory.swap` field gets (skipped without swap accounting, like the memory swap test)
- when `unified` and the `memory` and `cpu` fields set the same file, the `unified` value wins
- a key for a controller that is not present makes `create` fail and leaves no container behind

The spec does not say which value should win in the third case. youki applies `unified` after the other fields, as runc does, and the test holds it to that order: `memory.max`, `cpu.max` and `cpu.weight` are set both ways with different values.
